title: Models and Interpretation in Predicate Logic

blocks.text: How can we determine if a mathematical statement is true or false within a specific context? Predicate logic provides the tools to interpret such statements.

blocks.markdown: In predicate logic, understanding the concepts of models and interpretations is crucial for evaluating the truth of logical formulas. A model provides a specific context or 'world' in which we evaluate these formulas.

blocks.title: Model
blocks.text: A model in predicate logic consists of a domain of discourse and an interpretation function that assigns meanings to the symbols in the language.

blocks.markdown: The domain of discourse is the set of objects that our variables can refer to. The interpretation function assigns each constant to an object in the domain, each predicate to a relation on the domain, and each function symbol to a function on the domain.

blocks.title: Interpretation
blocks.text: An interpretation in predicate logic assigns a meaning to the non-logical symbols (constants, functions, predicates) of the language.

blocks.markdown: To determine if a formula is true in a model, we evaluate it under the given interpretation. This involves checking if the relationships and properties described by the formula hold in the model.

blocks.title: Evaluating a Quantified Formula
blocks.prompt: Consider the formula $\forall x (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$ in a model with domain \{1, 2, 3\}, where $P(x)$ is true for $x = 1$ and $x = 2$, and $Q(x)$ is true for $x = 2$ and $x = 3$. Is the formula true in this model?

steps.text: Evaluate $P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)$ for each element in the domain.
For $x = 1$: $P(1)$ is true, $Q(1)$ is false, so $P(1) \rightarrow Q(1)$ is false.
For $x = 2$: $P(2)$ is true, $Q(2)$ is true, so $P(2) \rightarrow Q(2)$ is true.
For $x = 3$: $P(3)$ is false, $Q(3)$ is true, so $P(3) \rightarrow Q(3)$ is true.
The formula $\forall x (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$ is false because it is not true for all elements in the domain.

blocks.answer: The formula is false in this model.

blocks.markdown: Now, let's explore how to construct models that either satisfy or falsify a given formula. This involves selecting a domain and defining interpretations that make the formula true or false.

blocks.title: Constructing Models
blocks.prompt: Construct a model that satisfies the formula $\exists x (R(x) \land S(x))$ and another that falsifies it. Assume $R(x)$ and $S(x)$ are predicates.

steps.text: To satisfy $\exists x (R(x) \land S(x))$, choose a domain where at least one element makes both $R(x)$ and $S(x)$ true.
Model 1: Domain = \{a, b\}, $R(a)$ = true, $S(a)$ = true. $R(b)$ = false, $S(b)$ = false. The formula is true because $R(a) \land S(a)$ is true.
To falsify $\exists x (R(x) \land S(x))$, ensure no element makes both $R(x)$ and $S(x)$ true.
Model 2: Domain = \{a, b\}, $R(a)$ = true, $S(a)$ = false. $R(b)$ = false, $S(b)$ = true. The formula is false because no element satisfies $R(x) \land S(x)$.

blocks.answer: Model 1 satisfies the formula, while Model 2 falsifies it.

blocks.title: Validity vs. Truth
blocks.text: A formula is valid if it is true in every model, whereas it is true in a particular model if it holds under that specific interpretation.

points: Models provide a context for evaluating the truth of predicate logic formulas.
Interpretations assign meanings to the symbols in the language, determining truth values.
Distinguishing between validity and truth in a model is crucial for logical reasoning.
